content: The Institute for Polyacrylate Absorbents (IPA) has established specific guidelines to assist its member companies in managing worker exposure to fine polyacrylate polymer dust, particularly in the micrometer size range. These guidelines emphasize the use of engineering controls and safe work practices to minimize exposure risks. The ability to control worker exposure to carbon nanotubes (CNT) and carbon nanofibers (CNF) below a respirable mass concentration of 1 µg/m³ as an 8-hour time-weighted average (TWA) is currently uncertain. However, achieving this level of control is likely feasible in most manufacturing and end-use tasks if appropriate engineering controls are implemented and workers are adequately trained in the safe handling of CNT and CNF materials. Until research studies can fully elucidate the physical and chemical properties of CNT and CNF that determine their inhalation toxicity, all forms of CNT and CNF should be treated as respiratory hazards. Consequently, exposures should be minimized to the lowest possible levels, ideally below the recommended exposure limit (REL). The REL is based on the respirable airborne mass concentration of CNT and CNF because adverse lung effects observed in animal studies occurred in the alveolar region, where gas exchange takes place. The term respirable refers to the aerodynamic size of particles that, when inhaled, can deposit in the alveolar region of the lungs. Sampling methods have been developed to estimate the airborne mass concentration of respirable particles. Using a respirable elemental carbon (EC) mass-based REL provides a practical approach to identifying job tasks with potential CNT and CNF exposures, enabling the implementation of appropriate measures to limit worker exposure. Recommendations Based on current scientific evidence from experimental animal studies regarding the hazard potential of CNT and CNF, it is recommended to establish an occupational health surveillance program. This program should include both hazard surveillance and medical surveillance components. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) advises employers and workers to take the following steps to minimize potential health risks associated with CNT and CNF exposure: 1. Substitution: Whenever possible, replace CNT and CNF with nonhazardous or less hazardous materials. 2. Engineering Controls: When substitution is not feasible, prioritize the use of engineering controls to reduce worker exposure to CNT and CNF. 3. Criteria for Engineering Controls: Develop and implement criteria and procedures for selecting, installing, and evaluating the performance of engineering controls to ensure they operate effectively. Examples include exhaust ventilation systems. 4. Routine Exposure Evaluation: Regularly assess airborne exposures to verify that control measures are functioning correctly and that worker exposures remain below the NIOSH REL of 1 µg/m³. This can be achieved using NIOSH Method 5040, as outlined in Section 6 and Appendix C of the guidelines. By following these recommendations, employers can better protect workers from the potential respiratory hazards posed by CNT and CNF.
